This isn't a scene from a film. This is a heartbreaking reality that still exists in parts of Nepal. For some women and girls, getting their period means being sent away from their own home to spend the night in a small shed, away from their families. They are left to face cold nights, fear, loneliness, and the danger of snakes, insects, and wild animals—all because of a natural biological process. Menstruation should never be a reason for exclusion or shame. Take a moment and ask yourself: If it were someone you love—your daughter, your sister, your wife, or your mother—would you accept this as "tradition"? Some customs deserve to be questioned, especially when they put lives and dignity at risk. Every woman deserves to feel safe, respected, and valued, no matter what day of the month it is. Let's raise awareness, start conversations, and stand together to end harmful practices like this. Replying to @char🪩 CYCLONE UPDATE 2 👀 There is a cyclone hitting Nepal in the next few days so we are now stuck at our current tea house (places you stay on the trail) as the government has warned for people not to trek due to risk of flooding, landslides & avalanche 👀 We are safe & way above any rivers or potential land side. So fingers crossed everyone if safe 🤞 We were meant to be here one night but we are now here for at least 3, before hopefully continuing on towards the goal of summiting Mera Peak.  If we are able to continue the trek it means missing out an acclimatisation day & rest days before the summit push so it will be TOUGH! For now wishing everyone stays safe.  Will by @rab.equipment.uk  jacket withstand the rain 👀 @rab.equipment  & thank you Garmin for proving my altitude.
